papers.title_in_file: Contextuality and inductive bias in quantum machine learning
papers.what_it_is: A preprint that defines contextuality for multi-task learning models, proves that a noncontextual model class encoding a linear conserved-quantity bias is limited in expressivity, and compares a biased quantum model with classical surrogates on a rock, paper, scissors toy problem.

existing.value: The authors state that contextuality is tied to expressivity: contextual model classes that encode the inductive bias are generally more expressive than their noncontextual counterparts.
quotes: A consequence of this connection is that contextuality is tied to expressivity
contextual model classes that encode the inductive bias are generally more expressive than their noncontextual counterparts
existing.certainty_reason: An author's summary claim in the abstract; the supporting result is Theorem 4.1, for one bias.

existing.value: The authors state that a pertinent open question for this work is whether the linearly conserved quantities they consider can be usefully encoded in classical models using a tractable amount of resources.
quotes: Perhaps the most pertinent question regarding this particular work is whether the linearly conserved quantities we consider
(for potentially larger label dimension) can be usefully encoded in classical models using a tractable amount of resources.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 10 Outlook, p.31: the paper states it as an open question.

existing.note: The comparison is a numerical study on small simulated quantum models; the authors state they do not claim quantum advantage.
existing.value: The authors state that, on an explicit toy problem based on learning the payoff behaviour of a zero-sum game, quantum learning models with the associated inductive bias outperform their corresponding classical surrogate models, and that they do not claim this is evidence of quantum advantage since the quantum models are small enough to be easily simulated on a laptop computer.
quotes: we construct an explicit toy learning problem
show through our toy problem that they outperform their corresponding classical surrogate models
based on learning the payoﬀ behaviour of a zero-sum game
We stress that we are not claiming that this is evidence of
since the quantum models we consider are small enough to be easily simulated on a laptop computer
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The paper defines a noncontextual ontological model of an operational scenario as a triple of ontic states, ontic state distributions and ontic response functions that satisfy the constraints (16) and (17) and reproduce the operational statistics.
quotes: of ontic states, ontic state distributions and ontic response functions satisfying the constraints (16) and (17) such that

assertions.value: The paper defines a multi-task model as noncontextual iff the operational statistics of its associated operational scenario admit a noncontextual ontological model, and as contextual if no such model exists.
quotes: admits a noncontextual ontological model. If such an ontological model does not exist, the learning model is said to be contextual.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Section 3, p.11.

assertions.value: The paper states that its definition of contextuality applies to a single trained multi-task model h(theta) rather than being a property of the entire model class.
quotes: Our deﬁnition of contextuality will apply to h(θ) rather than be a property of the entire model class H.
assertions.certainty_reason: Scope of the definition, Section 3, p.10.

assertions.value: The paper poses the learning problem with a linear bias: a data set with labels in {-1, 1}^m whose expected labels satisfy a sum constraint, for which a multi-task model must sample the marginal conditional distributions for unseen inputs.
quotes: samples from the m marginal conditional distributions D(y(k)|x)
assertions.certainty_reason: Problem statement, Section 4.1, p.11.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 4.1: for a multi-task model that encodes the bias (28), if the set V2/3, the convex hull of the points ui(eta) for eta equal to 2/3, is strictly contained in the convex hull of the model's set of behaviours V, then the multi-task model is contextual in the sense of Definition 3.2.
quotes: Theorem 4.1: Necessity of contextuality for biased multi-task models
Consider a multi-task model {Pθ1(y|x), Pθ2(y|x), Pθ3(y|x)} that encodes the bias (28). If the set V2/3 given by the convex hull of points

assertions.value: The paper states that, in contrapositive form, a multi-task model that encodes the bias and is noncontextual has a convex hull of possible behaviours that cannot contain V2/3, which limits the expressivity of noncontextual multi-task model classes.
quotes: the convex hull of possible behaviours cannot contain V2/3. This amounts to a limit on the expressivity of noncontextual multi-task model classes
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct corollary of Theorem 4.1, stated in Section 4.1, p.13.

assertions.value: The authors state that for certain data sets the expressivity limit may impact the generalisation ability of the model class, for example when many test inputs have ground truth behaviours close to the six extremal points.
quotes: For certain data sets this may impact the generalisation ability of the model class
all models in the class will struggle to approximately sample the correct label distributions on some of the inputs, which may hinder generalisation ability
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' hedged statement (may), not tested for noncontextual classes.

assertions.value: The paper derives that equally mixing the preparation density pairs (s1, s2), (s3, s4) and (s5, s6) each gives a preparation returning uniformly random labels for the three tasks, so the three mixtures are operationally equivalent.
quotes: equally mixing any of the pairs of preparation densities (s1, s2), (s3, s4), or (s5, s6) results in another preparation density that returns uniformly random labels for the three tasks
These mixtures are therefore indistinguishable and we have the operational equivalences

assertions.value: The paper sets up a three-player variant of the rock, paper, scissors game with a referee, in which the expected payoff of Player k is given by the number of players it beats minus the number that beat it, and the payoffs are probabilistically decided.
quotes: The payoﬀs are decided probabilistically based on the actions of the players.
is equal to the number of players that Player k beat in that round minus the number of players that beat Player k.
assertions.certainty_reason: Game definition, Section 5.1, p.17.

assertions.value: The paper states that the rock, paper, scissors game is zero-sum, so its data distribution satisfies the bias that the sum of the three expected payoffs is 0 for all strategies x, and any data set built from a zero-sum game in the same fashion satisfies it.
quotes: any data set constructed from a zero-sum game in the same fashion will satisfy (67).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.2, p.18-19.

assertions.value: The paper defines the problem of learning the payoff behaviour of a zero-sum game: from a data set of strategies and payoffs that respects the zero-sum bias, construct a multi-task model that samples from the marginal payoff distributions for unseen strategies.
quotes: samples from the marginal payoﬀ distributions D(y(k)|x) for unseen strategies x.
assertions.certainty_reason: Problem statement, Section 5.3, p.19.

assertions.value: The paper states that no noncontextual multi-task model satisfying the zero-sum bias can sample the correct payoff distributions for all possible strategies, and that it fails for some strategies near the deterministic strategies that give the six extremal behaviours.
quotes: no noncontextual multi-task model that satisﬁes the zero-sum bias will be able to sample the correct payoﬀ distributions for all possible strategies
assertions.certainty_reason: Application of Theorem 4.1 to the RPS problem, Section 5.3, p.19.

assertions.value: The paper defines a learning model as noncontextual relative to a bias if the operational statistics of the scenario restricted to the preparations and the effects that appear in the bias admit a noncontextual ontological model.
quotes: The learning model is noncontextual relative to the bias (77) if the operational statistics of the operational scenario
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Section 6.2, p.21.

assertions.value: The paper states that for a joint model, considering the full set of preparations and effects may give no preparation equivalence, so contextuality may not be provable even if the coarse-grained multi-task model is contextual.
quotes: As a result, the ontological model will lack the constraints implied by these equivalences, and we may be unable to prove contextuality
assertions.certainty_reason: Argument in Section 6.1, pp.20-21, with an example in Appendix C.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the state-based approach a bias-invariant layer must use unitaries from the set G, a matrix Lie group whose Lie algebra is the Hermitian operators X that commute with the bias operator H.
quotes: It follows that the bias H is conserved by any data-encoding unitary of the form
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement in Section 7.1, p.23.

assertions.value: The authors state that they are unaware of general methods to construct parameterised unitaries in the set that prepares states satisfying the bias, and rely on ad-hoc approaches.
quotes: We are unaware of general methods to construct parameterised unitaries in G
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit, Section 7.1, p.23.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the measurement-based approach, three equally spaced trine observables in a plane of the Bloch sphere satisfy the bias for a qubit and m equal to 3, that observables of this form for larger dimension are not known, and that Appendix D gives a construction for m equal to 3 for all even dimensions.
quotes: observables of this form for larger dimension are not known
In Appendix D we give a previously unknown construction for the case m = 3 for all even dimensions that satisﬁes (89).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit and scope, Section 7.2, p.24.

assertions.value: The paper gives, in Appendix D, a construction of three observables with eigenvalues plus or minus 1 that sum to 0 in every even dimension d at least 2, from projections P and Q whose difference squared is a fixed multiple of the identity.
quotes: set of three ±1 valued observables Ok in even dimension d that satisfy the zero-sum bias condition O1 + O2 + O3 = 0 for all even d ≥ 2
Therefore, the corresponding observables satisfy the desired bias.
assertions.certainty_reason: Construction stated and checked in Appendix D, p.38.

assertions.value: The authors use a three-qubit quantum model class with bias operator H equal to the sum of the Pauli Z operators on the three qubits, built with the state-based approach, and train it on the RPS data set of 1500 strategies.
quotes: The bias operator for this ansatz is H = σz1 + σz2 + σz3.
containing 1500 strategies xi ∈ Dx and payoﬀs yi.
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup of the experiment, Section 8.1 and Figure 7 caption, p.25.

assertions.value: The authors define the classical surrogate as three linear Fourier features models with the same frequency spectrum, passed through a HardTanh function, and state that the surrogate does not encode the zero-sum bias and that they could not identify how to enforce it.
quotes: The surrogate model does not however encode the zero-sum bias
we were unable to identify a general method that would scale to larger label dimensions
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup and stated limit of the comparison, Section 8.3, p.27.

assertions.value: The authors train by minimising the negative log likelihood with the Adam optimiser and evaluate by the average KL divergence between model and true marginal label distributions, estimated on 10000 test strategies, and state that the training method does not scale well for quantum models.
quotes: We sample N = 10000 strategies xitest via D(x)
We acknowledge that this training method does not scale well for quantum models
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup, Section 8.4, p.28.

assertions.value: The authors report that, among the four model classes (the biased quantum model, a generic quantum model and two surrogates), the best test KL divergence is achieved by the biased quantum model, which they conclude is due to its ability to encode the zero-sum bias.
quotes: The best performance is achieved by the biased quantum model class however, which we conclude is due to the ability of the quantum model to naturally encode the zero-sum bias.
The best performance is achieved by the biased quantum model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the cause is the authors' conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiment does not isolate the bias by ablation within one architecture; the unbiased quantum model has a different structure.

assertions.value: The authors report that the surrogate models suffer from over-fitting, that adding an L2 weight penalty alleviated the over-fitting but did not improve generalisation performance, and that they suggest the quantum model's lower error comes from the inductive bias rather than over-fitting in the surrogate.
quotes: Although this alleviates the problem of overﬁtting, we did not ﬁnd that it improved generalisation performance
This suggests that the lower generalisation error of the quantum model over the surrogate originates from the inductive bias rather than overﬁtting in the surrogate model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the surrogate models are able to outperform a generic quantum model class, as has been observed before.
quotes: the surrogate models are able to outperform a generic quantum model class
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, consistent with a cited earlier observation.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not claim their numerical result is evidence of quantum advantage, since the quantum models are small enough to be easily simulated on a laptop computer.
quotes: We stress that we are not claiming that this is evidence of
since the quantum models we consider are small enough to be easily simulated on a laptop computer
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Section 8, p.24.

assertions.value: The paper states that for zero-sum games with larger payoff dimension a similar operational equivalence can be identified, which constrains a noncontextual ontological model, and that a clear picture of how these constraints affect learning is needed.
quotes: This will limit the expressivity of the model as before, however a clear picture of the structure of these constraints and how they aﬀect learning is needed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated open problem, Section 9.1, p.29.

assertions.value: The authors state that their framework is not the only option nor the most general possible, and name extensions: contextuality for transformations and a definition taken with respect to the full model class.
quotes: the framework we present here is by no means the only option, nor the most general framework possible
assertions.certainty_reason: Scope statement, Section 9.4, p.30.

assertions.value: The authors state that an alternative way to view the value of quantum machine learning may be through the ability to parameterise expressive model classes that encode certain data structures, rather than in terms of computation.
quotes: perhaps an alternative way to view the value of quantum machine learning is not in terms of computation, but through the ability to parameterise expressive model classes that encode certain data structures
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion, not tested beyond the toy problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the nonlinearity of neural networks makes it difficult to impose linear constraints on the nonlinear output variables, whereas the linear structure of quantum theory enforces the linear bias.
quotes: it becomes diﬃcult to impose linear constraints on the nonlinear output variables [64]
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement supported by a citation, not by a result in this paper.

assertions.value: The paper argues that taking the physical theory as the operational scenario makes contextuality depend on physical details irrelevant to model behaviour, because a quantum model simulated with diagonal states and measurements has no preparation equivalences and so can never exhibit contextuality.
quotes: In the absence of preparation equivalences it is impossible to have generalised contextuality
assertions.certainty_reason: Argument in Appendix A, p.36.
